planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70F; Louisiana Short is a late, stocky heirloom that keeps branching and setting fruit through the season, so a longer sowing window into early summer still gives a strong fall crop in zone 9.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the soil is thoroughly warm, since this late-season heirloom needs the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to hit its stride. Louisiana Short produces stocky, heavily branching plants bearing short, fat, dark green pods that stay tender at a larger diameter than slim-podded types, so pods can be picked at 3-5 inches without turning woody. The compact branching habit keeps fruit within easy reach and yields hold up right until a hard frost, making it one of the more forgiving okra choices for gardeners who cannot pick every single day during peak heat. Originally maintained by an Oklahoma seed saver and preserved through Midwest heirloom seed banks, it performs reliably in the humid, clay-heavy soils common along the Gulf Coast.

common_name: My Joanie Okra (Mississippi Heirloom Pink-Blushed Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70F; My Joanie is a Mississippi heirloom on compact 4-foot plants that trialed as an early producer despite its late-variety reputation, making it a good fit for the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season.

directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep once soil is reliably warm; harvest pods at 3-4 inches every couple of days to keep plants productive. My Joanie is a Mississippi heirloom okra passed along through home gardeners before being preserved by Midwest seed-saving growers, distinguished by a dusky rose blush that washes over its grass-green pods rather than the solid red found in burgundy-type okra. Plants stay a manageable 4 feet tall and hold up well in a Kerr Center trial of heirloom okra varieties, where it out-yielded many taller types despite being marketed as a late producer. The mix of ornamental color and heavy yield makes it a good double-duty choice for a Gulf Coast vegetable bed that also needs to look good.
sources: Kerr Center for Sustainable Agriculture — Heirloom Okra Variety Trial

common_name: Perkins Dwarf Okra (Compact Southern Heirloom Long-Pod Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Perkins Dwarf is an early, compact strain of the classic Perkins okra line, reaching only 3-5 feet, so it fits small Gulf Coast beds and containers better than the tall Perkins Long Pod and Perkins Mammoth Long Pod types.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm; harvest at 3-5 inches for the most tender eating, though pods stay usable up to 8-9 inches longer than most okra. Perkins Dwarf is a compact-growing strain within the old Perkins okra family, bred down from the tall Southern heirloom standard to a manageable 3-5 foot plant while keeping the same ribbed, dark green pods and early, heavy production. The shorter stature means less staking and easier picking through the peak of a Gulf Coast summer, and the extended window of pod tenderness gives more forgiveness if a hot spell delays harvest by a day or two. It remains an excellent choice for canning, pickling, and frying, and its early start lets Gulf Coast gardeners begin harvesting well before many full-size heirloom types come into production.
sources: Victory Seed Company — Perkins Okra Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Easy Gardening: Okra

common_name: Granny Franklin Okra (Alabama Heirloom Frying Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Granny Franklin is an Alabama family heirloom bred for heavy, reliable yields through the long, humid Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep once the soil is warm; pick pods every 1-2 days at 3-4 inches for the most tender texture. Granny Franklin is an Alabama family heirloom, kept going for generations by home gardeners specifically for its heavy, consistent yield of classic green pods and its reputation as an outstanding frying okra. The tall, vigorous plants shrug off the intense heat and humidity that stress many other vegetables through a Deep South summer, continuing to set pods reliably as long as they are harvested regularly. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saved from healthy plants breeds true, letting Gulf Coast gardeners maintain their own line of this regional variety year after year.
sources: Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Growing Okra in the Garden

common_name: African White Eggplant (Small Round Ivory Heat-Tolerant Eggplant)

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; transplant only once nights stay reliably above 55F. African White is a tropical African heirloom that thrives in the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer and can be kept over as a short-lived perennial in zone 9-10.

directions: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into warm soil once nights are reliably above 55F; harvest fruit while still glossy white and firm, since pods age to yellow and then red as they overripen and lose their mild flavor. African White is a tropical African heirloom eggplant that produces abundant clusters of small, round, ivory fruits on a vigorous, glossy-leaved plant that doubles as an attractive ornamental in a mixed vegetable bed. The 2-3 inch fruits have a mild, faintly nutty flavor and few seeds when picked young, making them good for quick sautes, curries, and pickling. Because it hails from hot equatorial growing conditions, African White tolerates the extended heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer better than many standard purple-fruited types, continuing to set fruit through the stretch of the season when cooler-adapted eggplants slow down.

common_name: Cambodian Green Giant Eggplant (Southeast Asian Heirloom Striped Round Eggplant)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; transplant once nights stay warm. Cambodian Green Giant is a Southeast Asian heirloom bred for hot, humid tropical conditions and ramps up production in the second half of a long Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay warm; harvest fruit while pale green with dark green stripes and firm, before the skin dulls and seeds enlarge. Cambodian Green Giant is a Southeast Asian heirloom producing large, round, slightly flattened fruit striped in pale and dark green on compact 2-3 foot plants, giving strong yields relative to the space the plant occupies. The dense, full-bodied flesh holds its texture well on the grill or in a wok, a quality suited to the quick high-heat cooking common in Southeast Asian cuisine. Because it is bred for tropical growing conditions, it handles the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer with ease and produces most heavily from midsummer into fall, right as many spring-planted eggplants begin to decline.

common_name: Illikomban Eggplant (Kerala Heirloom Long Green Snake Eggplant)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55F. Illikomban is a Kerala backwater-region heirloom bred for tropical heat and humidity, well matched to a Gulf Coast summer, and benefits from a sturdy stake or cage to support its long fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 55F; harvest fruit young and glossy for the sweetest flavor and most tender texture. Illikomban is a rare heirloom from the Onattukara backwater region of South Kerala, India, named for its resemblance to an elephant tusk and prized for producing glossy, light green fruit that can reach two feet or more in length. The silky, nearly seedless flesh has a sweet, nutty flavor that cooks down quickly, making it well suited to curries and stir-fries where the fruit is sliced and absorbs bold spices readily. As a variety selected for tropical growing conditions, it takes the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer in stride, continuing to set long fruit through the hottest stretch of the season when many Western eggplant types slow production.
